title: Need a notary? here’s how eNotarization works in the Philippines
summary: MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos can now have digital documents notarized online. The Supreme Court began offering electronic notarization (eNotarization) on Monday, October 19, 2026, through three…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos can now have digital documents notarized online. The Supreme Court began offering electronic notarization (eNotarization) on Monday, October 19, 2026, through three accredited platforms: Twala, QLegal and NotarizeIT.
An electronically notarized document has the same validity, force and effect as one notarized under the 2004 Notarial Rules, and it can be relied on to the same extent.
The system is expected to make notarization more accessible to people who face geographic and logistical barriers to traditional notarial services.

What is online notarization?

Online notarization, or eNotarization, is a digital process in which an electronic document is signed and notarized through a secure Electronic Notarization Facility, with an Electronic Notary Public administering the act.
Instead of printing a document and visiting a notary’s office, the signatory completes the notarization on an accredited online platform.

Under the Rules on Electronic Notarization, digital documents in PDF or PDF/A format can be notarized by video call, in person, or a combination of both, with a commissioned notary located anywhere in the Philippines.
What to prepare
Every platform requires the same two things: a valid, unexpired Philippine National ID or other government-issued ID, and the document as a PDF or PDF/A file.

For the session, users need a device with a working camera and microphone, an internet connection of at least 2 Mbps per user, an up-to-date browser such as Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox, and an email address for account creation and notifications.
VPN, proxy and Tor connections must be switched off because they can interfere with location verification. Electronic notarization covers four types of notarial act:

Acknowledgment. Signatories declare they signed voluntarily. It applies to deeds of sale, lease agreements, powers of attorney, commercial contracts, board resolutions, loan agreements and promissory notes.

Jurat. A person swears that a statement is true. It applies to affidavits and sworn statements, and to court verifications and certifications of non-forum shopping where the court or receiving agency accepts them electronically.
Oath or affirmation. A solemn declaration or pledge, such as an oath of office.
Signature witnessing. The notary attests to seeing the signature. It covers authorizations, consent forms and liability waivers.
Documents that require wet signatures cannot be eNotarized. These include notarial wills, depositions and paper instruments signed by hand.

Users should also confirm that the office receiving the document accepts it. Shortly before the launch, the Supreme Court signed joint circulars with the Land Registration Authority and the Securities and Exchange Commission so that both can accept electronically notarized land and business documents.
For title transfers, it is worth checking whether the local Registry of Deeds still requires wet-ink copies.
How to get a document eNotarized
1. Register with an accredited facility
Choose one of three Supreme Court-accredited facilities: Twala, QLegal or NotarizeIT. On the Court’s registration portal, select your facility and create an account on its site.
The screenshots below show Twala. Those marked as illustrations come from Twala’s eNotary page and use sample data. QLegal and NotarizeIT will look different.

blocks.caption: The Court’s registration portal. Select a facility to create an account.
Twala’s sign-in page. Sign in with eGovPH, Apple, Google, Microsoft, single sign-on or email.
The Twala dashboard, with Create envelope and a Notarizations menu.

blocks.text: 2. Choose an Electronic Notary Public
Pick a lawyer from the Court’s list of commissioned ENPs.
3. Upload your document
Upload your file as a PDF or PDF/A and keep your ID ready. Do not sign by hand. On Twala, everyone signs electronically through an envelope first, and the notary is told when it is ready.

blocks.caption: Twala’s Create new envelope window. Name the document, choose Remote or In person, and upload your file. Use a PDF or PDF/A, as the Court’s rules require.
Signing (illustration). Everyone signs through the envelope before the notary is told the document is ready.

blocks.text: 4. Complete identity verification and appear before the notary

Verify your identity with your ID. The notary confirms that everyone understands the document and is signing voluntarily. Use the accredited platform. Zoom, Google Meet and Microsoft Teams are not allowed.
You and any witnesses appear before the Electronic Notary Public by video call, in person, or a combination of both, depending on the signing method you chose.

Twala verifies identity once. Each principal and witness submits a photo of an unexpired ID, or a Philippine National ID checked against the national registry, plus a face scan. Verification requires consent and a fee, and lasts until the ID expires, up to three years.

blocks.caption: The session (illustration). The notary, principal and witness join one video call. A checklist confirms the details before payment is requested.

blocks.text: Remote sessions run in the browser. Twala says the signer can join from anywhere, including overseas, but the notary must be in the Philippines. VPN, proxy and Tor are blocked, and the session is recorded only if everyone consents.
5. Receive your e-notarized document
The notary applies an electronic signature and Electronic Notarial Seal. You can download your e-notarized document right away, and a copy goes to the Supreme Court’s Central Notarial Database.

blocks.caption: The Notarizations page tracks your documents.

blocks.text: The notary requests payment by link, due within 24 hours. Once paid, Twala adds the certificate and seal and files the entry with the Supreme Court. Check any notarized document on Twala’s verification page.
Where to get help

The Supreme Court has posted instructional videos that show how to use each facility, along with the requirements for each platform. For questions or concerns, send them through the Electronic Notary Services Helpdesk Form.

With eNotarization now live, getting a document notarized no longer requires a trip to a notary’s office. You register with an accredited facility, choose a commissioned notary, verify your identity and complete the session online, and your e-notarized document is ready to download, with a copy filed in the Supreme Court’s Central Notarial Database.
Documents that need wet signatures still cannot be eNotarized, so check your document and the receiving office’s requirements before you start.
The system is expected to make notarization more accessible, especially for people who face geographic and logistical barriers.
